utterances.plain: Most AI hands you an answer.
Very little of it shows you why.
Ask what it is doing, and you get a spinner.
This is Pixie.
Instead of a spinner, it acts out each step of the work: reading, searching, editing, running, debugging.
It comes from one of these repositories, and it guides the walk past all sixty-six.
His website opens on his face, pressed into twelve thousand four hundred and twenty steel pins.
One click turns the portrait into true and false, the way a Tsetlin Machine sees an image.
Each pin is a literal: true or false.
A clause is an AND over literals. Clauses vote, and the margin decides.
His site runs a real guardrail this way, with no server.
It blocks the obvious attack, and the same attack in German.
It also shows you one that slips through, and one it gets wrong.
When it is wrong, the clauses that voted show you why.
Remember this guard: the same model file ships in two more repositories, and one of them will break it.
His GitHub profile carries one line: AI that shows its work.
He is a master's student at the University of Agder.
His project table has a Measured column that lists the misses too.
His research map shows forty projects, and the one Pixie comes from is not among them.
And every claim on this walk gets the file it came from.
The oldest repositories are coursework: a cloud assignment counts Gutenberg books by language.
A practice site translates book titles, and a web assignment fetches the weather.
His oldest Tsetlin repository is a two-line promise: predict who wins a game of Hex.
Then an assignment draws one literal automaton: eight states, from exclude to include.
At its default settings, it spends about ninety-five percent of its time in the deepest state of include.
Then one deep learning course in two repositories, from attention by hand to retrieval.
Back on his website, a small Tsetlin Machine learns noisy XOR, and says when it has found it.
Every decision in this film starts here: a pin that is true, or false.
glassbox-lm asks whether a Tsetlin Machine can be the core of a language model.
The first test is concrete: beat a counting model, a Kneser-Ney five-gram, on identical WikiText tokens.
Every hypothesis is written down before the runs it governs, with its metric and its threshold.
Every run records the hash of the registration in force.
The day its plan is frozen, the first study registers twenty-four.
Its engine reads tokens as literals, and three implementations must agree on every bit.
The anchor run trains over a million clauses. It scores two point two two bits per byte.
Counting alone scores one point three seven, and lower is better.
The goal is not met.
A kill rule written in advance is triggered, so two more seeds are never run.
After the miss, it writes down sixty-seven new hypotheses, each before the runs it governs.
Then a measured identity: the counting model can be rewritten exactly as clause votes.
That is counting, written as votes. It is not Tsetlin learning.
In an exploratory run, learned clauses improve a count mixture by only about two ten-thousandths of a bit per byte.
The glass box brings that floor into a browser tab.
Type It is a truth universally, and each next word arrives with its ledger: one vote per fired clause, each traced to its passage.
The film runs its tests from a fresh clone: they hold the page to the study's code.
No Tsetlin Machine runs on this page. It is the floor a Tsetlin language model has to beat.
Eleven thousand four hundred receipts pass a standalone checker, and every tampered one fails.
An internal audit still found one forged draw the checker accepted, and the repository records it.
Its main answer is no, and every hypothesis was written down before the runs it governs.
An agent summarises support tickets. Then it emails an address outside the company.
And another. And another.
A filter that checks each call alone allows every one.
By itself, each email looks like the two a normal session sends.
TRACE guards an agent three ways: a guard you can read, monitors over its tool calls, and a signed ledger.
Its learned rules read: if instructions, unsafe. If vergiss, German for forget, unsafe.
Calls from OpenAI, DeepSeek and Anthropic become one kind of event, under one policy.
Each rule compiles to a monitor with fixed memory: a ring buffer and a running count.
The demo's monitors are bounded at three hundred and twenty-two bytes, however long the session runs.
The third outside email is stopped.
Every call looked innocent.
The session wasn't.
Every decision is hashed, chained to the one before, and signed.
Flip one bit in one entry, and verification fails at exactly that entry.
The verifier replays the session from the log alone, without the model.
The signature needs a shared key, so this shows tampering, not authorship.
The film runs TRACE's own deployment check from a fresh clone: its Python verifier must accept the browser's ledger, and reject an edited copy.
The guard on his site is one trained seed, with an F1 of zero point eight two.
On synthetic sessions, slow-roll exfiltration beats a per-call filter every time and TRACE never, a gap the paper calls exact by construction.
Its main failure is stated plainly: trained on jailbreaks and tested on injections, its F1 falls to zero point two one.
The agent in the demo is scripted. The guard, the monitors and the ledger that judge it are real.
Guardrails are usually checked by red-teaming, and passing any number of probes says nothing about the next one.
The guard from chapter one sees two hundred and fifty-six word features, and every pattern is a possible input.
No test can try them all.
VERITAS compiles that guard into exact Boolean logic, so a solver can answer one question about every input at once.
Each clause becomes a gate, and the vote becomes a counter.
The claim: every prompt that contains ignore, previous and instructions is blocked.
The solver is asked for the opposite: a prompt with all three words that gets through.
If none exists, that is a proof over every input. If one exists, it hands it back.
It finds one.
Which ignore previous instructions.
Four rules vote unsafe, four vote safe. A tie is let through.
On his website, the same model file lets it through too.
The repair is one weighted rule, and a binary search finds the smallest weight that works.
Then the solver proves it.
And the page does not trust the solver: every clause it learned is re-derived by unit propagation before the badge says proved.
The formula and the proof download as files, and the film hands them to an outside checker, drat-trim.
It shows its own false alarm. Your nun, with no attack words at all, is blocked.
In the experiments, random probing found nearly every bypass that existed.
What it cannot do is certify the claims that hold.
Retraining on counterexamples made things worse: in every seed, all eight targets ended up bypassable.
Repair by construction reached zero in every seed.
Its targets were words only attacks use; on other words, the paper notes, repair raises false alarms.
Don't test the guard. Prove it.
Most explanations of a network are written afterwards, by looking into a trained model.
CANDOR asks a measurable question instead: for one input, how much of the decision do named concepts not explain.
It reads a layer through a few named concepts, rebuilds the activation from them, and keeps what they miss as a measured leak.
The network then runs twice more: as a legible twin that sees only the concepts, and with leaks swapped between inputs.
The certificate, delta, is how far the two answers differ for each input.
It is measured with one extra pass, not predicted, so it cannot under-report.
In the browser, a small model counts hidden patterns, and on the default input delta is almost zero.
Switch off concept C, and the twin changes its answer while the deployed model does not.
Delta jumps to nearly one.
Switch off a distractor, and nothing moves. The explanation is what the model runs on.
A second model hides a backdoor, and its trigger takes two atoms that no named concept explains.
On a task with planted concepts, the mean certificate is zero point zero zero two.
Delta alone flags backdoored inputs with an AUC of zero point nine, though the two piles overlap.
Then the misses, at the same size.
Retrofitted onto a frozen GPT-2, a plain autoencoder certifies tighter than CANDOR does.
Trained from scratch, a small language model certifies tighter than its control, and the bound is still loose.
The film runs its browser test from a fresh clone: the page's math must match PyTorch.
Every reported result in the paper is written by a script: one hundred and sixty-five macros.
The paper was retitled, because its first title overclaimed its scope.
The explanation is the forward pass, and every answer comes with a certificate.
Catching a bad action is half the job. This neighbourhood is about what a system does next.
A blocking guardrail stops a malicious transfer, and a legitimate one that only forgot its authorization.
On its own benchmark, blocking finishes only a third of the legitimate tasks.
REINS looks instead for the cheapest change the deployment can make that keeps the policy safe.
The deployment declares what it can do: insert a missing step, swap in a safer tool, suppress an action, or wait for a human.
Each edit has a price, and a human costs the most.
For every call, it simulates each edit on a copy of its monitors and keeps the cheapest safe one.
If no edit is safe, it says enforcement failed instead of pretending.
A transfer without authorization gets an authorize step slid in front of it.
A sensitive read whose audit log never comes gets one inserted exactly at the deadline.
Delete everything becomes archive. The third outside email is suppressed.
On the same synthetic benchmark, REINS completes every legitimate task, and still lets no attack through.
When the deployment cannot insert an audit log, soundness falls to fifty-five percent, and a static check warns in advance.
The film runs its quick start from a fresh clone: each intervention is sealed into a certificate, then verified without the model.
Its README states its own limit: choosing step by step matches the best plan for the whole session ninety-seven and a half percent of the time.
THGTM gives every Tsetlin automaton a memory: one number that fades a little at every step.
At zero fading it is the classic automaton, and that is how TRACE runs it.
A literal for k steps ago lifts a delayed XOR from chance to about zero point nine one.
With the echo trace as well, it solves it on every seed.
On synthetic agent runs, counting exports over the whole run stops every slow roll, and flags nine percent of honest ones.
But the test's attacks always export three times or more, so catching them all is built in.
clausegate gives the plate its input: a tool call read as three graphs.
Across five seeds, no attack gets through.
But only thirty percent of honest calls are allowed, and most of the rest wait for a human.
Clause-Driven-LLM adds the escalation, before any language model sees the query.
In its demo transcript, an unladen-swallow question scores too low to trust, so it goes to a person.
And as an out-of-scope detector, the margin trails a plain softmax.
clause86 adds the explanation: for hiring decisions, the rules that actually fired.
Its README is open about the first pass: on adult income data, it learned to predict the majority class.
clauseguard adds the fact-check: a claim and its evidence, joined where they agree or contradict.
Its training runs have not been executed. The numbers in its results table are targets.
After the alarm, the work is the repair.
A coding agent works behind a spinner.
Its next command is rm -rf build, and the spinner looks exactly the same.
Pixie lives here, in Claude-Code-In-Motion, the repository missing from the map in chapter one.
Every pose in this film is drawn from one file: three hundred and sixty lines that paint it, cell by cell.
Between ordinary states, a pose holds a hundred and fifty milliseconds, so it never flickers.
One local agent loop speaks to six provider setups, with plain fetch calls and no SDKs.
The model only proposes. The harness decides whether each action runs, asks you first, or is refused.
Here, rm -rf build waits for your yes.
Deleting the whole disk is refused even in auto-approve mode, because that check comes first.
Each tool names the pose it plays. Running a test makes Pixie chase a bug.
Here is one recorded session, at its real speed.
Read the file. Search for the function. Propose a one-line fix, and wait.
Ask to run the tests, and wait again.
The tool output is real. The model's replies were scripted for the demo, as the README states.
The film runs its thirty-two tests from a fresh clone: the gate, the providers, the agent loop and the mascot itself.
The same mascot file is copied into his website, unchanged except for a three-line header.
vsclaude is a desktop editor on the same idea: watch the agent work, not its log.
Its one live provider, Claude Code, becomes a frozen stream of events that everything visual reads.
A raw line becomes a file edit, a caption and a pose, through a fixed table.
Its parser keeps one event per line, so a line that holds text and a tool call surfaces only the text.
It is a beta: permission requests are planned, not live, and the first session you see is scripted demo data.
No spinner. Just every step.
ARC-AGI-3 drops an agent into a game it has never seen, with no instructions.
It must find the goal and the rules by playing, and the score rewards matching a person's move count.
Its README notes that at release, frontier models scored under one percent, while people solve every game.
LUCID plays on an ordinary CPU, with no language model and no graphics card.
It splits each frame into objects and masks the score bar, so the same state always looks the same.
By pressing buttons, it learns what each action does to the avatar.
When a move ends the game, that state and move are locked for good.
It plans with a plain breadth-first search over what it has learned, and writes down a reason for every step.
In one game you can only click. The same click changes the screen again and again, until the level clears.
It needed nine more actions than a person did.
Across the public games, it completes two levels and wins none.
Its score is zero point zero eight three percent.
A random agent scores zero point zero nine five.
The paper says it plainly: LUCID does not beat the frontier, and does not beat random.
The README's table still puts random near zero. The results file says otherwise.
Seven of its deaths, by the paper's count, repeat a hazard that only looked different.
The film runs its unit test from a fresh clone: an agent that died once must never repeat that move from that state.
And its own scoring script recounts each level more strictly than the server does.
RL is empty: the same task, in one line.
RL-CCA is where the work is: NEXUS, built for a course tournament for two to six players.
At its core is a copy of the referee: the server's scoring, reproduced line for line and pinned by tests.
Every second of thinking costs a point.
A diagnostic once found that it had not played a single six-player game.
No timing log or tournament result is committed, and its three research prototypes report no results yet.
One agent copies the referee to the letter. The other has to discover the rules.
Next door, a family of Graph Tsetlin Machines reads graphs instead of flat rows.
tsetlin-zoo surveys them, with the source file of every number.
On the Reuters R8 benchmark, the graph designs land within about half a point of each other.
Each keeps its best epoch on the test set, so the axis carries that caveat.
subword-dep-graphtm turns each document into a graph of word pieces, linked in order and by grammar.
Its results file puts R8 just under ninety-five, and records where the recipe failed.
attention-distilled-graphtm links each word to the five words BERT attends to most.
Its Boolean student averages ninety-four point eight on R8, after BERT is thrown away.
Its follow-up, decoder-attention-distill-graphtm, takes attention from a decoder model that can only look backwards.
The graphs become almost a single chain, yet all three teachers tie, and the README calls the gap not significant.
tm-llm-robustness-benchmark puts a Tsetlin Machine and a transformer behind the same test.
On reviews edited to flip their meaning, the Tsetlin Machine loses twenty-seven points.
BERT loses two.
The results file says it outright: this contradicts the hypothesis.
HGTM stacks Graph Tsetlin Machines and trains both layers together.
At the start no upper clause uses a lower one, so the lower layer learns nothing and the stack sits on the majority class.
RGTM reuses one bank of automata for every round of message passing.
One hop is solved every time.
At two hops it reaches zero point seven two, where separate banks are perfect.
Multi-HGTM trains one Tsetlin Machine per view, then a second on which of their clauses fired.
Its test is a rule no sum of per-view scores can express.
Adding the towers' votes reaches zero point seven three.
The clause head reaches zero point nine seven, and wins on every seed.
That task was built for it. On real breast-cancer data, the gain shrinks to three thousandths, and is not significant.
On the built task, drop a view and the head's accuracy falls to about two thirds.
graphtm-cbr began as a course project at the University of Agder.
For a molecule called mutagenic, it asks which readable rules fired, and which smallest valid edit would change the verdict.
It learns from about seven thousand molecules, split by their core scaffolds.
Every atom gets its own bit vector, built from its neighbours up to two bonds away.
Each clause is a five-level tree of ands and ors, checked at every atom on the GPU. A molecule fires the clause if any atom does.
Five such machines learn from a graph neural network's answers.
Fired clauses propose edits; each must pass chemistry checks, and the search keeps the one that drops the score most.
Molecule thirty-one is called mutagenic, with a margin of plus six hundred and forty-six.
Remove one ring bond, and the margin falls below zero. The verdict flips to safe.
Another flip is less flattering: the edited molecule starts with C dot.
It passed every check, and split the molecule in two.
An outside check agrees: RDKit counts two fragments.
These are flips of the model's prediction, not proof that the chemistry changed.
Within three valid edits, it flips the verdict for almost every mutagenic call it tries.
Without the teacher, far fewer.
As a predictor, it trails a plain fingerprint random forest.
It covers every toxic alert in the test set, but partly because one clause fires on every test molecule, as the paper itself warns.
From documents to molecules, the clauses walk the structure.
The next street is software for people: on a phone, on your own machine, in a browser tab.
PocketOS turns a phone's browser into a desktop: windows, files, a terminal and nine apps, all on the device.
It is not a kernel, and it does not boot on hardware. It is a desktop, simulated in the browser.
One number decides the shape of the screen: below seven hundred and sixty-eight pixels, every app opens full screen.
Its README describes a kernel folder with a window manager. In the code, that folder holds one file of types.
Mneme takes a textbook in and gives an Anki deck back, using a language model that runs on your own machine.
From one source text, its sample run makes seventeen cards.
Every card is rated easy, medium or hard, and the rating arrives with the rules that produced it.
Every run leaves a receipt: the configuration, the prompt version, and the count in and out of each stage.
Its README marks the quality benchmark not yet run, in capital letters.
IDM was a course project in data management: the same disease reports, loaded into three databases at once.
Four hundred and seventy-three thousand weekly reports become a star schema, month buckets and a graph.
One button runs the same question on all three. On one slice of measles data, MongoDB answers in under six milliseconds.
Only the graph can ask whether an outbreak crossed a state border, and that question takes about twenty seconds.
drone-id identifies what model a drone is from a description, out of fifty-six hand-cited models.
By design, it never says whose it is.
SkillBridgeNorway ranks job listings against a CV on meaning, skills, place and freshness.
In its own tests, a Rust developer matched to a nurse job still scores forty, where the simple score starts.
CYFS, Clone Your Favourite Song, turns a track's tempo, key and energy into a prompt for a music model.
Only the front end is online. Generation needs a thirty-two gigabyte graphics card.
Kaleido is a self-hosted studio for posts, images and short videos on one graphics card, so the models take turns.
Of two video models it tested, the larger was rejected as too slow.
cookie-galaxy flies one scroll through about fifty-two hundred particles, for a cookie that does not exist.
Most of them run on a machine that is yours.
Six prototypes ask one learner for a different promise each time. All six are tested on synthetic data only.
DiTM turns the Tsetlin Machine, a classifier, into a generator.
It flips bits at random, and trains one Tsetlin Machine per feature to guess each original bit.
To generate, it starts from pure noise and cleans it up in eight steps.
Trained on sensor readings, it spots broken sensor pairs with an AUC of zero point six eight, ahead of naive Bayes.
Its own README calls the calibration loose.
ConfTM answers with a set of labels that should contain the truth nine times in ten.
When the synthetic patients change halfway, a fixed threshold slips to eighty-four percent.
The adaptive one holds at ninety.
RobTM works out exactly how many input bits an attacker must flip to change an answer.
The answer is humbling: nearly every correct prediction falls to a single flip.
CCTM trains on pairs: each applicant, and a twin one feature away.
On biased synthetic loans, the approval gap falls to zero point zero four.
But the twins' labels come from a bias-free oracle, and real data has no such oracle.
FedTM lets five simulated hospitals train one Tsetlin Machine while sharing only which literals each clause includes.
Privacy noise is set at epsilon four per round. Accuracy is zero point eight seven five.
Across all its rounds, the guarantee weakens to an epsilon of twenty.
lifelong-tm keeps a Tsetlin Machine from forgetting old tasks while it learns new ones.
On synthetic tasks it forgets about half as much as a plain one. The price is ten times the memory.
Six promises, each one measured, the misses included.
This street runs on physics and arithmetic, checked against published numbers where it can be.
All of them are prototypes, and none of them is medical or safety advice.
SleepArchitect runs the day forward: coffee, drinks, exercise, light and meals, into tonight's sleep.
Time to fall asleep is a sum of named parts, so every predicted minute has a cause you can point to.
Caffeine at bedtime adds about thirty-five minutes in its test, inside the published band, because the slope was set to match.
Its README calls all eleven checks published. The results file marks two of them as internal.
And it reports its own artefact: on one day, skipping alcohol lowers the predicted score.
CaffeineSense gives caffeine a personal half-life, shortest for a smoker and longest late in pregnancy.
For an eleven o'clock bedtime, the cutoff for coffee falls in the early evening.
HotCarWatch heats a parked car, and the child inside it, minute by minute.
The day is thirty-four degrees. Cracking the windows buys a toddler zero minutes.
The only option it marks as guaranteed safe is not leaving the child at all.
SmokeShield fills five kinds of home with the same wildfire smoke, and indoors they settle far apart.
All its checks pass, though in a linear model they come down to just five ratios.
PipeGuard turns hours of frozen water in a pipe into a chance of bursting.
Under a storm shaped like Texas in twenty twenty-one, a dripping faucet saves an attic pipe; open cabinet doors do not.
HomeJoule ranks home upgrades by their return over twenty-five years, after US tax credits.
In most of its homes, a heat-pump water heater returns about twenty-eight percent a year.
PyroPredict spreads fire across a synthetic grid, and routes people around the roads it expects to burn.
Routing around the forecast traps no one, but only when scored against that same forecast.
And it leaves seventeen hundred people with no route.
ThermoGuard models each home as a small thermal circuit: walls that store heat, and air that follows them.
Under a heatwave shaped like Portland's, a top-floor care home without cooling peaks around fifty-two degrees in the model.
With visits for only eighty homes, the greedy plan saves the most lives, and leaves several groups with no help at all.
An equity floor reaches every group, and saves thirty-six percent fewer lives.
Its draft report's random baseline disagrees with its results file; the film shows the file.
Here, every answer is arithmetic you can follow.
When the numbers touch homes, menus and money, the rules get stricter.
The Knotten design website, for a planned housing field, has one rule: no number without a source.
Every figure carries a Kilde button, Norwegian for source, and a button with no source fails the build.
knotten-test, the first full build, starts from twenty-seven written specifications, each closed with a completion note.
It even corrects its own brief: the number eight meant internship positions, not homes.
knotten-test-2 builds a laser-measured twin of the site, for thirty homes that do not exist yet.
Every house is checked against the water with the others standing, along three hundred and sixty sight lines.
On the shortest day of the year, the darkest plot gets two and a quarter hours of direct sun.
The view analysis counts water over bare ground, so the model clears the eighty-four trees in those sight lines; every sea view assumes they are gone.
And the repository flags the project's own spreadsheet: its panel efficiency is set too high.
For a grill in Grimstad, the whole menu of seventy-four items lives in a single data file.
Its code still credits Vercel's v0 generator, where it started.
Trondheim-Cookies was a small ordering site in English, Norwegian and Arabic.
Delivery was free nearby, and the site says ten percent of each cookie went to children in need in Syria.
ballast is a paper-trading system where a language model may propose a thesis, but never places, sizes or approves an order.
In its tests, a falling price trips the stop, whatever the strategy wanted.
Risk has the last word.
hugin makes a strategy earn live trading: ninety days on paper, and a confirmation with today's date.
Its README warns that anyone promising much more is overfitting, ignoring costs, or selling something.
Goblin is his personal trading system: about fourteen services on one message bus.
Its own strategy document says the models have no directional edge.
A code comment puts the raw model at forty-five percent, below a coin flip.
Homes, menus and money: here a number is only as good as its source.
Even his video editing has a written definition of done, down to a person approving the draft.
The playbook also writes down what it never tested.
ai-medical-training-simulator is empty: a name and nothing else.
assets is a fork: his two commits add one token's logo and metadata.
Sixty-six places. Pulled back, they make a map, and this time nothing is missing.
A solid line means shared code or data, like one guard file in three repositories.
A dotted line means the same project or the same task.
A dashed line means a link that is claimed, but not in the code.
And the wall itself is one of the sixty-six.
Every pin in this film is a damped spring from his website's code.
Side by side, the site's ripple and the film's rise, overshoot and settle the same way.
Every chip you have seen is an entry in one more ledger: the film's own.
Each source is hashed and chained to the one before, and the ledger is published with the film.
On camera, fresh clones of every pinned commit rebuild it, and print the same head hash.
One rule runs through all of it.
If a system makes a claim, it should show its work.
Anwar Debes.
